title: A Friendly Neighborhood Repair Shop Down The Street Quietly Overcharged My Trusting Eighty-Two-Year-Old Grandfather $4,700 For Brakes, Struts, And Engine Work On His 2008 Buick That Was Never Actually Done, Not Realizing His Granddaughter I
excerpt: My grandfather is 82. He’s driven the same 2008 Buick for fifteen years.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — THE BUICK
My grandfather is 82. He’s driven the same 2008 Buick for fifteen years.

It’s a silver LaCrosse with a dented rear bumper from a run-in with a mailbox in 2016 and a fuzzy steering wheel cover my grandmother bought him before she died. He keeps a box of tissues on the dashboard, a bag of butterscotch candies in the cup holder, and a St. Christopher medal clipped to the visor.

His name is Frank Moretti. He worked thirty-eight years as a machinist at a tool and die shop in Youngstown, Ohio. He can still tell you the tolerance on a part by feeling it with his thumb. He raised four kids, buried a wife, and has nine grandchildren.
I’m one of them. My name is Jessica, but everyone calls me Jess. I’m twenty-six.

I’m an ASE-certified mechanic. I’ve worked at a dealership service department in Boardman for six years. I got my first set of wrenches from Grandpa when I was eight. He taught me how to change oil in his driveway, lying on a piece of cardboard, with him pointing a flashlight and telling me “lefty loosey, righty tighty” over and over.
My mother wanted me to be a nurse. Grandpa told her to let me do what I loved.
“The girl’s got good hands, Marie,” he said. “Let her use them.”

Grandma Teresa used to say that Grandpa loved that Buick almost as much as he loved her. He washed it every Saturday morning, rain or shine, in the driveway with a bucket and a chamois. After she died, he kept washing it. He told me once it gave his hands something to do on the loneliest day of the week.

When I passed my ASE certification tests, Grandpa framed the certificate and hung it in his living room, right next to his own retirement plaque. He tells everybody at church that his granddaughter “fixes cars better than any man in Mahoning County.”
PART 2 — THE STRANGE NOISE
Last month, he took it to a repair shop near his house for a “strange noise.”
Grandpa didn’t call me. He never wants to bother me. He says I work hard enough all week without fixing his car on my days off.

So he drove to a small repair shop on Market Street, about a mile from his house. It had a big sign that said “Senior Discount Every Day” and a smiling cartoon mechanic giving a thumbs-up. He’d driven past it a thousand times.
He told the man at the counter that the car was making a rattling noise underneath, especially when he went over bumps.
The man said they’d take a look. He gave Grandpa a ride home in the shop’s van.
Brakes, rotors, a new transmission flush, “engine decarbonization,” a fuel system cleaning, front-end alignment, and new struts.

The man on the phone talked fast and used a lot of words Grandpa didn’t understand. He said the brakes were “metal on metal” and “very dangerous.” He said the struts were “completely shot.” He said the engine was “full of carbon” and could fail at any time. He said, “Sir, I wouldn’t let my own grandmother drive this car.”

Later, Grandpa told me the man had also said the car’s “check engine computer” was showing “serious warnings.” The Buick’s check engine light wasn’t even on. When I asked Grandpa if he’d seen any paperwork showing those warnings, he said no. The man just told him over the phone.
Grandpa paid it. He didn’t want to argue. He’s from a generation that trusts a man who works with his hands. And he didn’t want to bother me.
PART 3 — I FIND OUT

I stopped by Grandpa’s house on a Sunday afternoon to bring him a tray of my mother’s lasagna. While he was making coffee, I noticed a receipt stuck to his refrigerator with a magnet shaped like a cannoli.
I read it twice. I felt my face get hot.
He looked embarrassed. “Oh, the Buick needed some work. They said it was dangerous. I didn’t want to bother you.”
“Four thousand seven hundred dollars?” I said. “Grandpa, that car is worth maybe four thousand dollars.”
“They said the brakes were metal on metal,” he said. “They said the struts were shot.”

I read the receipt more carefully. Brake pads and rotors, front and rear. Four struts. Transmission flush. Engine decarbonization service. Fuel system cleaning. Alignment. Plus “shop supplies” and “environmental fees.”

I’ve seen a lot of repair bills. I write them myself every day. Some of those charges were reasonable on paper. But all of them, on a fifteen-year-old Buick that an eighty-two-year-old man drives twice a week to church and the grocery store?
Grandpa didn’t tell me because he didn’t want to bother me. When I finally heard, I drove over and popped the hood.

I asked him if they’d given him his old parts back. He said they’d offered to “dispose of them for free.” I asked if he’d seen the car on the lift. He said no, he’d waited at home. I asked if anyone had shown him the worn brakes. He shook his head. Every answer made my stomach tighten.
Actually, I didn’t have to drive over. I was already there. I just went out to his garage, opened the door, and grabbed my flashlight from my truck.
PART 4 — UNDER THE HOOD
I got the Buick up on ramps in Grandpa’s garage, the same garage where he taught me to change oil when I was eight.
Grandpa sat on his old stool with his coffee and watched me work, just like he used to.
First, I looked at the brakes. I took off the front wheels.

The brake pads weren’t new. I could see the wear lines. And on the back of the pads, there was a manufacturing date stamp. The “new” brake pads had a dirty, worn edge and a date stamp from 2019. They’d been on the car for years.
The rotors weren’t new either. They had the same scoring patterns and rust ridges I’d expect on rotors that had been there for a long time.
Then I looked at the struts. The struts had fifteen years of rust on them. The original factory struts, as far as I could tell. Nobody had touched them.
I checked the transmission fluid. It was dark and old. Not freshly flushed.
I couldn’t verify the “engine decarbonization” or the “fuel system cleaning” just by looking. Those are services where a shop pours chemicals into the engine or the fuel system. But I had my doubts.
Most of the parts on the bill had never been replaced.

I slid under the car with my flashlight. Near the exhaust pipe, I found a heat shield, a thin piece of metal that protects the underside of the car from exhaust heat. One of its mounting clamps had rusted through. The shield was loose and rattling against the exhaust pipe.

I also checked the alignment with a simple tape measure and a straight edge. It was close enough, but there were no marks on the tie rods showing anyone had adjusted them. The car had driven straight for fifteen years. No one had touched it.
The strange noise? A loose heat shield. A five-dollar clamp. I fixed it in ten minutes with a clamp I had in my truck.
PART 5 — THE CALL I DIDN’T MAKE
I came out from under the car and sat on the garage floor. My hands were shaking. Not from cold. From anger.
“Grandpa,” I said, “they didn’t do the work. Most of it, anyway. The brakes are old. The struts are original. They charged you for parts they never put on.”
He didn’t say anything for a long time. He looked at the Buick. Then he looked at his hands. Machinist’s hands. Hands that spent thirty-eight years making parts to the thousandth of an inch.
“Thirty-eight years I made parts,” he said. “I never once sold a man a part he didn’t need. Never once.”
I didn’t yell. I didn’t call the cops. Not yet.
I wanted to. Believe me. I wanted to drive straight to that shop and throw the receipt in the owner’s face.

But I’m a mechanic. I know how this works. If I accused them, they’d say Grandpa was confused. They’d say the parts were replaced and I was wrong. They’d say I was a girl who didn’t know what she was talking about. I’ve heard that one before.
I needed proof. Not just of what they did to Grandpa. Proof of what they do.
Grandpa put his hand on my shoulder. “Whatever you do, Jessie,” he said, “do it right. Do it so nobody can argue.” That’s how he made parts. That’s how I decided to handle this.

So I took photos of everything. The brake pads with the date stamp. The rusty struts. The old transmission fluid. The broken heat shield clamp. Then I wrote down the date and time on a notepad and had Grandpa sign it, like a witness.
PART 6 — THE GOPRO
I called the shop and made an appointment for my own car.

I drive a 2015 Honda Accord. I keep it in perfect condition, because that’s what mechanics do. New brakes six months ago, which I installed myself. New struts last year. Fresh fluids. Everything documented with receipts and photos.
